title: Hempstead: Colonial Claims and Native Challenges
summary: English settlers used a Dutch colonial patent to build and govern Hempstead. Native people later challenged payment and the authority claimed over their land. Deeds, colonial institutions and Native objections tell different parts of this regional history.
address_label: Hempstead, North Hempstead and coastal islands — modern regional context

why_this_matters: A patent strengthened settler government without resolving Native objections. Naming the people who challenged payment and another sachem’s authority makes clear why a colonial paper title is not the whole history of this homeland.

history_title: Agreements, colonial authority and Native challenges
history_content:
A homeland larger than Hempstead village

Hempstead in this history is not simply today's village. Colonial claims reached across the central plains, north-shore country and southern meadows. The surviving 1643 deed copy names Masepeage, Merriack and Rockaway people. Woods, grasslands, marshes and waterways were connected places of livelihood and community life. A map of later town claims must be read beside Native objections, rather than taken as proof that everyone agreed to surrender the whole landscape. Documents Relative to the Colonial History of New York, volume XIV, pp. 530 and 696

English settlers and Dutch colonial authority

Robert Fordham and John Carman were English settlers negotiating for people coming from Stamford, Connecticut. Their agreement was followed by a patent from Willem Kieft, the Dutch director-general of New Netherland, in November 1644. Hempstead's early settlers were English, but their town initially operated under Dutch colonial government. The town archive identifies a further confirmation in 1657. These were different stages: an agreement, a colonial charter and a later confirmation—not one act that explains every subsequent claim. History of the Town

How a patent strengthened settler control

On November 16, 1644, Dutch director-general Willem Kieft issued the patent to Robert Fordham, John Stickland, John Ogden, John Carman, John Laurence and Jonas Wood and their associates. It claimed authority through the Dutch States General, Prince of Orange and West India Company. The text described land and waterways around the Great Plains, between named bays and extending north to south; it also linked settlement rights to bringing families into the area. Long Island Colonial Patents, pp. 145–146

The patent authorized the settlers to build towns and establish local government. It promised protection of their property against rival European powers and required payments to the colonial administration after a stated interval following peace with Native people. These provisions show how a claimed transfer could acquire institutions, settlement and imperial backing. A colonial charter was not itself proof that all Native owners accepted the claim: the 1675 hearing records their continuing objections. Long Island Colonial Patents, pp. 146–150; Documents Relative to the Colonial History of New York, volume XIV, pp. 696

What the surviving deed says—and cannot show

The copy printed from Carman family papers is dated November 13,1643; another tradition dates the agreement December 13. It describes half of the great plain toward the south side of Long Island, extending through woods, meadows, marshes and pasture. Its written terms provide for the purchasers and their heirs and assigns to hold the land permanently. Multiple Native marks appear, including the mark of the Masepeage sagamore. The copy does not name that sagamore in the signature line. Documents Relative to the Colonial History of New York, volume XIV, pp. 530

The text was itself copied from a damaged document. It refers to straight lines and a town location that cannot simply be plotted as modern property corners. The regional outline here therefore does not claim to reconstruct the 1643 deed. Nor does the colonial language let us recover every signer's understanding or prove later agreement with Hempstead's interpretation. Documents Relative to the Colonial History of New York, volume XIV, pp. 530

Native people challenged payment and authority

On August 5,1675, Tackpousha appeared in a hearing about Hempstead's occupation of Native land. Richard Gildersleeve Sr and George Hewlett represented the town. Tackpousha said the Mericock land enjoyed by Hempstead had not been paid for; the record also reports an offered payment considered insufficient. He challenged payment for both northern and southern land. Documents Relative to the Colonial History of New York, volume XIV, pp. 696

The town's defense invoked a Dutch governor's purchase and patent, compensation for livestock, conquest and a confirmation by a Montaukett sachem. Native speakers rejected that sachem's right to give away their land and maintained their nonpayment claim. These are competing arguments recorded in a colonial proceeding. The town's assertions should not be repeated as uncontested facts. The governor allowed time for the Native participants to consult others; this account does not record a final settlement. Documents Relative to the Colonial History of New York, volume XIV, pp. 696

From town claims to private beach interests

The southern meadows and beaches also became property that Hempstead claimed power to divide. In its 1898 decision in Lawrence v. Town of Hempstead, New York’s Court of Appeals traced a disputed Rockaway meadow and beach tract through town allotments in 1678, a 1725 conveyance to Captain Jacob Hicks and an 1878 partition sale. The majority accepted the private claimants’ chain against the town. This later contest did not establish Native consent to Hempstead’s original claim. Tackpousha’s 1675 objection belongs beside that later ownership record.

The case also shows why an old beach deed cannot simply be drawn over a modern map. Inlets and creeks had shifted, and the judges disagreed over the evidence. Its particular tract must not be equated with every marsh island or today’s entire Long Beach barrier. Lawrence v. Town of Hempstead, 155 N.Y. 297 (1898), majority opinion and dissent

Land was not only paper title

The hearing exposes a central problem in reading deeds: a document that settlers relied on could coexist with a continuing Native challenge to payment, authority and possession. Naming the people who objected restores their decisions and actions to a history often compressed into the word purchase. Permanent private title in colonial paperwork should not be confused with proof that Native relationships with land had ended. Documents Relative to the Colonial History of New York, volume XIV, pp. 530 and 696

Read the Hempstead Plains deed, Mercock land dispute, Matinecock homeland and Merrick homeland for connected histories.
whereintheworld_content: The outline follows modern Hempstead and North Hempstead land, their coastal islands, and the Long Beach barrier, including today’s separate City of Long Beach. It locates a regional history; it is not the 1643 deed boundary, a colonial survey, or a statement of present ownership. Modern town limits divide some coastal features. Shores, inlets and engineered land have changed; modern ground must not be read as an unchanged seventeenth-century coastline. The Rockaway tract discussed in the 1898 court case is not the whole shaded region. Historic claims toward Queens extended beyond this outline. Read the linked Hempstead Plains deed and Mercock dispute for specific documents and Native objections. NYS Civil Boundaries: modern towns
